questions.q: How many days are in a leap year?
questions.x: An extra day, February 29, is added about every four years because Earth takes roughly 365.25 days to orbit the Sun.

questions.q: Who is credited with patenting the telephone in 1876?
questions.x: Bell reportedly said the first words over a telephone to his assistant: 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.'

questions.q: Which holiday is known for carved jack-o'-lanterns?
questions.x: The custom began in Ireland and Scotland, where people carved turnips; pumpkins became popular in North America.

questions.q: What does the 'www' in a web address stand for?
questions.x: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at the CERN research center.

questions.q: Which company makes the iPhone?
questions.x: Apple unveiled the first iPhone in January 2007, combining a phone, an iPod, and an internet device.

questions.q: What is the official currency of the United Kingdom?
questions.x: The pound is one of the oldest currencies still in use, with roots going back over a thousand years.

questions.q: Which artist painted the Mona Lisa?

questions.q: Which flower is traditionally given on Valentine's Day?

questions.q: What does ATM stand for?
questions.x: The first modern cash machine was installed in London in 1967.

questions.q: Who co-founded Microsoft with Paul Allen?

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies stars and planets called?

questions.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?

questions.q: A word that means the same as another word is called what?

questions.q: Which of these words reads the same forward and backward?

questions.q: How many sides does a standard stop sign have?

questions.q: Which computer key deletes the character to the left of the cursor?

questions.q: What does GPS stand for?

questions.q: What does the 'PIN' in PIN code stand for?

questions.q: Which holiday is celebrated on July 4 in the United States?

questions.q: Which month of the year has the fewest days?

questions.q: Which vitamin does your skin produce when exposed to sunlight?

questions.q: About how many hours of sleep do most adults need each night?

questions.q: Which organ pumps blood around the human body?

questions.q: How many teeth does a typical adult have, including wisdom teeth?

questions.q: Which German inventor introduced movable-type printing to Europe in the 1400s?

questions.q: What does USB stand for?

questions.q: What does CPU stand for?

questions.q: What does PDF stand for?

questions.q: In which language is 'bonjour' a common greeting?

questions.x: Franklin proposed it in the 1750s after studying electricity, and it protected buildings from fire.

questions.q: Which businessman introduced the moving assembly line for cars in 1913?
questions.x: The assembly line cut the time to build a Model T from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes.

questions.q: What does the German word 'Volkswagen' mean in English?
questions.x: The company was created in 1937 to build an affordable car for ordinary families.

questions.q: Who created the Linux kernel in 1991?
questions.x: He began it as a hobby project while a student in Finland; today Linux powers Android and most servers.

questions.q: What is the name of the NASA rover that landed on Mars in 2021?
questions.x: It carried a small helicopter, Ingenuity, which made the first powered flight on another planet.

questions.q: How many moons does Mars have?
questions.x: Phobos and Deimos are small and lumpy and may be captured asteroids.

questions.q: Which comet returns to Earth's skies about every 76 years?
questions.x: Edmond Halley correctly predicted its return after studying earlier sightings.

questions.q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
questions.x: Arteries have thick, elastic walls to handle the pressure of each heartbeat.

questions.q: What is the typical resting heart rate range for a healthy adult?
questions.x: Very fit athletes can have a resting heart rate below 60.

questions.q: What two words made up the first text message, sent in December 1992?
questions.x: Engineer Neil Papworth sent it from a computer to a colleague's phone on the Vodafone network in the UK.

questions.q: Which engineer chose the @ symbol for network email addresses in 1971?
questions.x: Tomlinson sent the first networked email himself, and later said he could not remember what the message said.

questions.q: Which inventor patented the typewriter that popularized the QWERTY keyboard layout?
questions.x: The layout was designed to reduce jams by separating commonly paired letters on early machines.

questions.q: In what year did Apple launch the first Macintosh computer?
questions.x: Apple introduced it during the Super Bowl with a famous TV commercial, and it popularized the mouse and graphical interface.

questions.q: In the audio format name MP3, what does 'MP' stand for?
questions.x: MP3 is short for MPEG-1 Audio Layer III, named after the Moving Picture Experts Group standards committee.

questions.q: Which letter of the alphabet does not appear in the name of any US state?
questions.x: J appears in New Jersey, Z in Arizona, and X in Texas, but no state name contains a Q.

questions.q: What is a word like 'brunch' or 'smog' that blends two other words called?
questions.x: Lewis Carroll popularized the term in 'Through the Looking-Glass', using it for words like 'slithy'.

questions.q: What is a word derived from a person's name, like 'sandwich' or 'cardigan', called?
questions.x: The sandwich is named for the Earl of Sandwich, and the cardigan for the Earl of Cardigan.

questions.q: The word 'robot' comes from a Czech word meaning what?
questions.x: It was introduced by the 1920 play R.U.R. by Karel Capek, whose brother Josef suggested the word.

questions.q: The word 'quarantine' comes from an Italian phrase referring to how many days?
questions.x: Ships arriving in Venice in the 1300s had to wait 40 days, or 'quaranta giorni', before landing, to protect the city from plague.

questions.q: Halloween traditions trace back to an ancient Celtic festival with which name?
questions.x: Samhain marked the end of the harvest season and was celebrated at the start of November.

questions.q: Which Scottish poet wrote down the words of the New Year song 'Auld Lang Syne'?
questions.x: Burns sent it to a collection in 1788, noting that he had taken it down from an old man's singing.

questions.q: On which date is Boxing Day observed in the UK and several other countries?
questions.x: The name is thought to come from the old tradition of giving boxes of money or gifts to servants and tradespeople.

questions.q: What is the Japanese custom of viewing cherry blossoms in spring called?
questions.x: The word means 'flower viewing', and families gather beneath blossoming trees for picnics.

questions.q: Which festival marks the traditional new year in Thailand with water fights?
questions.x: It is held in mid-April, and splashing water symbolizes washing away bad luck.

questions.q: Which company that later became a phone maker began in 1865 as a Finnish pulp mill?
questions.x: It was named after the Nokianvirta river, and over the years it also made rubber boots and cables.

questions.q: Sony's name combines the Latin word 'sonus', meaning sound, with an English word for what?
questions.x: The founders liked 'sonny' as a nickname for a lively young person, and dropped one 'n' to make it easier worldwide.

questions.q: Which sportswear brand is named after the Greek goddess of victory?
questions.x: The brand's swoosh logo was designed in 1971 by a student who was paid $35.

questions.q: What is a market dominated by just a few large sellers called?
questions.x: Oligopoly comes from Greek words meaning 'few sellers'.

questions.q: Who wrote the 1776 book 'The Wealth of Nations'?
questions.x: Smith, a Scottish thinker, is often called the father of modern economics and wrote about the 'invisible hand' of markets.

questions.q: Which company was the first to issue publicly traded shares on a stock exchange, in Amsterdam in 1602?
questions.x: Investors could buy and sell its shares, creating the world's first stock market.

questions.q: The baht is the official currency of which country?
questions.x: A baht was originally a unit of weight for silver.

questions.q: Which country is credited with the first widely used paper money?
questions.x: Paper notes appeared in China around the 11th century, and Marco Polo later described them to astonished Europeans.

questions.q: In what year did euro banknotes and coins first enter circulation?
questions.x: The euro had existed as an electronic currency since 1999, but cash arrived on January 1, 2002.

questions.q: The Pareto principle suggests roughly what share of effects come from 20 percent of causes?
questions.x: Vilfredo Pareto noticed that about 80 percent of Italy's land was owned by 20 percent of its people.

questions.q: Which vitamin is also known as cobalamin?
questions.x: It contains the mineral cobalt and is found mainly in animal foods, so vegans often take supplements.

questions.q: Which is the smallest bone in the human body?
questions.x: The stapes, or stirrup bone, is inside your ear and is about the size of a grain of rice.

questions.q: How many pairs of ribs does a typical human have?
questions.x: The ribs form a protective cage around the heart and lungs.

questions.q: Which American researcher announced a successful inactivated polio vaccine in 1955?
questions.x: Salk famously refused to patent the vaccine, asking who could patent the Sun.

questions.q: In first aid, the acronym RICE stands for rest, ice, compression, and what?
questions.x: The method is used for sprains and strains, and raising the injured limb helps reduce swelling.

questions.q: Which disease did the World Health Organization declare eradicated worldwide in 1980?
questions.x: It is the only human infectious disease eradicated so far, thanks to a global vaccination campaign.

questions.q: Which moon of Jupiter is the largest moon in the solar system?
questions.x: Ganymede is larger than the planet Mercury, though it has less mass.

questions.q: Which planet takes longer to rotate once than to orbit the Sun?
questions.x: A Venusian day lasts about 243 Earth days, while its year lasts about 225.

questions.q: Who became the first American woman in space in 1983?
questions.x: Ride flew aboard the space shuttle Challenger and remains the youngest American astronaut to reach space.

questions.q: Who became the first American to orbit the Earth, in 1962?
questions.x: Glenn returned to space in 1998 at age 77 aboard the space shuttle Discovery.

questions.q: Which pair of NASA space probes launched in 1977 each carry a Golden Record of Earth sounds?
questions.x: The records hold greetings in 55 languages, music, and images, in case anyone finds them.

questions.q: Which star is the brightest in the night sky as seen from Earth, not counting the Sun?
questions.x: Sirius is also called the Dog Star, as it is part of the constellation Canis Major.

questions.q: In which year did astronomers officially reclassify Pluto as a dwarf planet?
questions.x: The International Astronomical Union made the decision at a meeting in Prague.

questions.q: How many Apollo missions landed astronauts on the Moon?
questions.x: Apollo 13 was meant to land but was aborted after an oxygen tank failed, and the crew returned safely.

questions.q: How many people have walked on the Moon in total?
questions.x: All twelve were Americans, and the last to leave the surface was Eugene Cernan in December 1972.

questions.q: Which Swedish-American engineer designed the modern zipper in the 1910s?
questions.x: His design was called the 'Hookless Fastener' before the name zipper stuck.

questions.q: Which DuPont chemist invented the strong fiber Kevlar in 1965?
questions.x: Kwolek noticed an unusual cloudy liquid that most chemists would have thrown away, and it led to a fiber five times stronger than steel by weight.

questions.q: Which Cornish engineer ran the first steam locomotive on rails in 1804?
questions.x: His locomotive hauled iron and passengers at a Welsh ironworks, but its weight broke the cast-iron rails.

questions.q: Which Scottish engineer improved the steam engine in the 1760s by adding a separate condenser?
questions.x: The unit of power, the watt, is named for him, and he popularized the term 'horsepower'.

questions.q: Which Scottish inventor gave the first public demonstration of a working television in 1926?
questions.x: His early system scanned images using a spinning disk with holes, and he showed it to members of the Royal Institution in London.

questions.q: Which French mathematician built one of the first mechanical calculators in 1642?
questions.x: He built it at age 19 to help his father, a tax official, with long sums.

questions.q: Which company released the 4004, the first commercially available microprocessor, in 1971?
questions.x: The tiny chip had about 2,300 transistors and was first designed for a Japanese calculator.

questions.q: Which US Navy rear admiral developed one of the first compilers, in 1952?
questions.x: Her work helped lead to the COBOL language and the idea that programs could be written in English-like words.

questions.q: Which architect designed the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, Spain?
questions.x: The titanium-clad building opened in 1997 and spurred the idea of a 'Bilbao effect' on tourism.

questions.q: Which Danish architect designed the Sydney Opera House?
questions.x: He won the design competition in 1957, but left the project before it was finished in 1973.

questions.q: Which engineer, famed for a Paris tower, designed the Statue of Liberty's internal iron framework?
questions.x: The sculptor Bartholdi designed the statue's exterior, and the flexible frame lets it sway in strong wind.

questions.q: In which country is the temple complex of Angkor Wat?
questions.x: It is the largest religious monument in the world and appears on Cambodia's national flag.

questions.q: What is the name of the giant sandstone rock in Australia's Northern Territory that is sacred to the Anangu people?
questions.x: It is also known as Ayers Rock, and visitors are no longer allowed to climb it.

questions.q: In which Spanish city is the Alhambra palace complex?
questions.x: The Alhambra was built mostly in the 1200s and 1300s and is famed for its intricate tilework and courtyards.

questions.q: Neuschwanstein Castle in Bavaria was built for which king?
questions.x: The fairy-tale castle inspired Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle, and Ludwig never saw it completed.

questions.q: Who was the first African American woman to travel into space, in 1992?
questions.x: Before becoming an astronaut, Jemison was a doctor and served in the Peace Corps in West Africa.

questions.q: Which Norwegian explorer led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in 1911?
questions.x: Amundsen's team beat Scott's British expedition by about five weeks, relying on sled dogs.

questions.q: Which self-taught Indian mathematician's life inspired the book and film 'The Man Who Knew Infinity'?
questions.x: Ramanujan wrote to the British mathematician G. H. Hardy in 1913, and Hardy invited him to Cambridge.

questions.q: Which artist painted 'The Persistence of Memory', featuring melting clocks?
questions.x: Dali painted it in 1931 and said the clocks were inspired by melting Camembert cheese.

questions.q: Which Dutch painter created 'Girl with a Pearl Earring'?
questions.x: Only about three dozen paintings by Vermeer survive, and the girl's identity is unknown.

questions.q: What is the fear of the number 13 called?
questions.x: The fear is why many tall buildings skip the 13th floor in their numbering.

questions.q: In the NATO phonetic alphabet, which word stands for the letter Q?
questions.x: The alphabet was designed so that each word sounds clearly different, even over poor radio connections.

questions.q: How many items are in a gross?
questions.x: A gross is a dozen dozens, and a 'great gross' is 12 gross, or 1,728.

questions.q: Which day of the week is named after the Norse thunder god Thor?
questions.x: Wednesday is named for Odin, Tuesday for Tyr, and Friday for the goddess Frigg.

questions.q: Which wedding anniversary is traditionally associated with paper?
questions.x: Traditional gift lists run from paper for the first year to cotton, leather, and iron in the following years.

questions.q: The Rosetta Stone, key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs, is displayed in which museum?
questions.x: Discovered in 1799, it carries the same decree in three scripts, which let scholars compare them.

questions.q: The word 'tsunami' comes from Japanese words meaning what?
questions.x: The name came from fishermen who returned to find their harbor devastated although they had felt nothing at sea.

questions.q: The word 'ombudsman', meaning an official who investigates complaints, comes from which language?
questions.x: Sweden created the first modern parliamentary ombudsman in 1809.

questions.q: At about what age did Louis Braille develop his raised-dot reading system?
questions.x: Braille became blind as a child, and he refined his system based on a military code of raised dots.

questions.q: Which Swiss businessman founded the Red Cross movement?
questions.x: Dunant was moved to act after seeing wounded soldiers at the 1859 Battle of Solferino, and he won the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.

questions.q: Which IBM engineer created the Ctrl+Alt+Del keyboard shortcut?
questions.x: Bradley made it as a quick way to restart a computer during development, and later joked that he may have invented it but Gates made it famous.

questions.q: The Python programming language was named after what?
questions.x: Creator Guido van Rossum was reading scripts from the British comedy show while he started the project in late 1989.

questions.q: Which tailor partnered with Levi Strauss to patent riveted work pants in 1873?
questions.x: Davis added metal rivets at stress points to make trousers last longer, and needed Strauss to pay the patent fee.

questions.q: The name Lego comes from a Danish phrase meaning what?
questions.x: The Danish phrase is 'leg godt', and Lego began as a wooden toy maker in 1932.

questions.q: Adidas is named after the nickname and surname of which German founder?
questions.x: His brother Rudolf founded the rival company Puma, after the two split in 1948.

questions.q: A lack of which mineral in the diet can cause a swelling of the thyroid gland known as goiter?
questions.x: Adding iodine to table salt, started in the 1920s, greatly reduced goiter in many countries.

questions.q: Which vitamin is essential for normal blood clotting?
questions.x: The K comes from the Danish word 'koagulation'.

questions.q: Which Hungarian doctor championed handwashing to reduce childbed fever in the 1840s?
questions.x: Death rates in his clinic dropped sharply after doctors began washing with chlorinated lime, but many colleagues dismissed his findings.

questions.q: What is the largest moon of Saturn?
questions.x: Titan has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane and ethane.

questions.q: Which inventor produced the first xerographic copy, the basis of photocopying, in 1938?
questions.x: Carlson's first copy said '10-22-38 Astoria', and it took years before a company would back his invention.

questions.q: Which Italian inventor sent the first transatlantic radio signal in 1901?
questions.x: The signal was the letter 'S' in Morse code, sent from Cornwall, England, to Newfoundland.

questions.q: Which Serbian-American engineer patented the alternating current induction motor in 1888?
questions.x: Westinghouse bought his patents, and AC power won the 'War of the Currents' against Edison's direct current.

questions.q: Which German physicist discovered X-rays in 1895?
questions.x: He called them X-rays because the 'X' stands for unknown, and he won the first Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.q: Earth Day was first observed in what year, on April 22?
questions.x: About 20 million Americans took part in the first Earth Day, which helped lead to the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency.

questions.q: Which small Spanish town hosts the annual tomato-throwing festival La Tomatina?
questions.x: Tens of thousands of participants throw ripe tomatoes in the streets for an hour each August.

questions.q: In which country is the Up Helly Aa fire festival held every January?
questions.x: The festival, held on the Shetland Islands, celebrates the islands' Viking heritage with torchlit processions and a ship burning.

questions.q: What is the dot above a lowercase 'i' or 'j' called?
questions.x: The word 'tittle' also gives us the phrase 'to the last jot and tittle'.

questions.q: The ampersand symbol (&) originated as a ligature of which Latin word?
questions.x: Et means 'and', and the symbol was once the 27th letter of the English alphabet recited by schoolchildren.

questions.q: Who created the constructed language Esperanto in 1887?
questions.x: Zamenhof, a Polish doctor, hoped a simple shared language would help people from different nations understand each other.

questions.q: Japanese writing combines hiragana, katakana, and which Chinese-derived characters?
questions.x: Hangul is the Korean alphabet, and romaji is the Latin-letter spelling of Japanese.

questions.q: Which Italian friar published a landmark 1494 book that described double-entry bookkeeping, earning the title father of accounting?
questions.x: Pacioli was also a friend of Leonardo da Vinci, who illustrated one of his books.

questions.q: Which banking family held great power in Renaissance Florence?
questions.x: The Medici bank was among the largest in Europe, and the family funded artists such as Botticelli and Michelangelo.

questions.q: Which company introduced the first general-purpose charge card in 1950?
questions.x: The idea reportedly came after its founder forgot his wallet at a restaurant dinner.

questions.q: What does the acronym RADAR stand for?
questions.x: The term was coined by the US Navy in 1940, and the technology was crucial for air defense in World War II.

questions.q: What does the acronym SCUBA stand for?
questions.x: The device was co-developed by Jacques Cousteau and Emile Gagnan in the 1940s.

questions.q: What does the acronym ASCII stand for?
a: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
Advanced System Code for Internet Interaction
questions.x: ASCII assigns numbers to letters and symbols, such as 65 for capital A, and it dates from the early 1960s.

questions.q: What does the acronym LASER stand for?
a: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Absorption by Standard Electron Resonance
questions.x: The first working laser was built by Theodore Maiman in 1960 using a ruby crystal.

questions.q: What does the 'HTTP' at the start of many web addresses stand for?
questions.x: The 'S' in HTTPS means the connection is secured with encryption.

questions.q: Interest earned on both the original amount and on previously earned interest is called what?
questions.x: Albert Einstein is often (probably wrongly) quoted as calling compound interest the eighth wonder of the world.

questions.q: Which Dutch company introduced the compact cassette in 1963?
questions.x: Philips made the format available to other manufacturers without charging royalties, which helped it become a worldwide standard.
